clinicalPearls: Presents with chronic watery diarrhoea, urgency, and sometimes nocturnal or postprandial stools, frequently misdiagnosed as diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome

Types are classically categorised as ileal disease/resection (type 1), idiopathic/primary from FGF19 deficiency (type 2), and secondary to other conditions such as cholecystectomy or coeliac disease (type 3)
Excess bile acids reaching the colon stimulate secretion and motility, producing the diarrhoea
The SeHCAT retention test, serum 7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one (C4), and fasting FGF19 are the principal diagnostic tools where available
A therapeutic trial of bile-acid sequestrants can be both diagnostic and treatment when testing is unavailable
First-line treatment is a bile-acid sequestrant, alongside identifying any underlying cause
Under-recognition is common, and many patients endure years of symptoms before diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: Bile acid diarrhoea results from an excess of bile acids entering the colon. Normally most conjugated bile acids are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and recycled; when this reabsorption fails (from ileal disease or resection) or when hepatic bile acid synthesis is inappropriately high (from impaired negative feedback by the ileal hormone FGF19), the bile acid load overwhelms colonic capacity. In the colon, bile acids stimulate electrolyte and water secretion and accelerate motility, producing secretory, urgent diarrhoea. Cholecystectomy and other conditions can also alter bile acid delivery and enterohepatic cycling.
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory bowel disease affecting the terminal ileum
additionalInvestigations: SeHCAT test to quantify bile acid retention where available
Serum C4 (7-alpha-hydroxy-4-cholesten-3-one) as a marker of bile acid synthesis
Investigations to exclude coeliac disease, microscopic colitis, and pancreatic insufficiency
Ileocolonoscopy with biopsies and imaging of the terminal ileum when structural disease is suspected
redFlags: Weight loss, rectal bleeding, or anaemia suggesting organic bowel disease
Nocturnal diarrhoea with dehydration or electrolyte disturbance
New change in bowel habit in an older patient requiring exclusion of malignancy
Features of malabsorption or inflammatory bowel disease
reference.prognosis: Most patients respond well to bile-acid sequestrants, though tolerability can limit adherence; symptoms tend to persist without treatment, and outcome also depends on any underlying disease.
pitfalls: Labelling the illness as irritable bowel syndrome without considering bile acid diarrhoea
Failing to test for or empirically treat bile acid malabsorption in chronic watery diarrhoea
Overlooking a treatable underlying cause such as coeliac disease or ileal pathology
Attributing sequestrant intolerance to treatment failure rather than adjusting therapy
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
British Society of Gastroenterology guidance on chronic diarrhoea
management: Bile-acid sequestrants (colestyramine, colesevelam or colestipol) as first-line treatment, which can also serve as a diagnostic therapeutic trial
Identify and treat any underlying cause, such as ileal Crohn's disease, coeliac disease, previous ileal resection or post-cholecystectomy change
A reduced-fat diet to lessen bile-acid-driven colonic secretion
Monitor and supplement fat-soluble vitamins where malabsorption is significant, and support adherence given the poor palatability of sequestrants
Consider a farnesoid-X-receptor agonist approach in refractory disease under specialist supervision
Gastroenterology referral for refractory symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty
